newsitem.title: ISRAEL: Israel to delay vote on capital market reform.
newsitem.headline: Israel to delay vote on capital market reform.

text.p: A panel set up to discuss a proposed tax on short and medium-term savings will not present its recommendations to the cabinet for a vote on Sunday as was originally planned, Treasury officials said.
Instead, the recommendations could be submitted to the cabinet on November 1.

The committee -- made up of the Treasury's director general David Brodett, Bank of Israel director David Klein and deputy director general of the prime minister's office Moshe Lion -- held its first meeting only on Wednesday. One reason for this was that Brodett was out of the country.
The panel will hold a second meeting on Sunday.

The panel, which is seeking a compromise to the Treasury's proposal to tax interest paid on savings of up to 10 years, was formed following a marathon cabinet meeting 10 days ago on capital market reform.

The savings tax is a crucial part of a package on capital market reform proposed by the Treasury. Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu, who took office in June promising not to raise taxes, led the cabinet in its decision to postpone a vote.

The Treasury is now recommending a tax of 3.5 percent on nominal interest paid on savings instead of the five percent originally proposed. Also, the tax would be levied only on savings of up to five years instead of 10.
Sources who were at Wednesday's meeting said that Lion, however, is opposed to this compromise. They quoted him as saying the ministers will not agree to any tax on savings.
The Treasury has argued that a tax on savings is needed to offset other parts of the reform package, such as lowering taxes on long-term savings and on dividends.
